new_statements.quote: 2.6. De dynamische klemtoon. In het algemeen ligt de klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep. Wellicht is dat ook het geval, indien deze een 'pepet' bevat. De voornaamwoordelijke syllabische suffixen beïnvloeden de oorspronkelijke klemtoon niet. Zo ligt zowel bij ina 'moeder', als bij ina-mu (inamu), 'uw moeder', de klemtoon op de eerste syllabe. [p. 26, 3.1.2:] De lengte van een syllabe heeft geen fonologische betekenis. ... ma-ma, 'zeer langdurig', waarin de beide delen lang zijn en gelijkelijk beklemtoond, tegenover mama, 'kauwen', waarbij de klemtoon op de eerste syllabe valt [p. 27, 4.3.1:] Een vrij groot aantal woorden is drielettergrepig. De eerste syllabe is niet beklemtoond.
new_statements.translation: 2.6. Dynamic stress. In general the stress lies on the penultimate syllable. Perhaps that is also the case when it contains a 'pepet' (schwa). The pronominal syllabic suffixes do not affect the original stress. Thus in both ina 'mother' and ina-mu (inamu) 'your mother' the stress lies on the first syllable. [3.1.2:] Syllable length has no phonological significance. ... ma-ma 'very long-lasting', in which both parts are long and equally stressed, versus mama 'to chew', where the stress falls on the first syllable [4.3.1:] A fairly large number of words are trisyllabic. The first syllable is not stressed.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate stress = penult); adds that pronominal enclitics are extrametrical (stress does not shift under cliticization), that schwa penults probably also take stress, and that length is non-phonemic. Consistent with the Balukh et al. 2024 sketch already held by the project (penultimate primary stress, clitics stressless).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (dynamic accent) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, probably also when the penult contains schwa; pronominal enclitics (-mu etc.) are outside the stress domain and do not shift stress (ina-mu keeps stress on i-, i.e. penult of the host); in trisyllables the first syllable is unstressed; vowel/syllable length is not phonemic; reduplicated monosyllables (ma-ma) carry equal stress on both halves.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described (only that the initial syllable of trisyllables is unstressed, and that full reduplications of monosyllables have two equal stresses).
new_statements.exceptions: Pronominal syllabic suffixes/enclitics do not count for stress placement (stress stays on the host's penult, so surface antepenult in ina-mu); author hedges ('wellicht') on penults with schwa; author warns (section 2) he is not phonetically trained and had only 7+5 days of exposure. Endnote 19 (p. 75) remarks that on a tape recording one form (kantu-wa) is heard with the last syllable stressed, suggesting the -wa is a separate clitic.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Komodo language (ata Modo speech) of Kampung Komodo on Komodo Island; Verheijen's data come from two short field visits with principal informant Magu and note recent West Manggarai influence on vowel realizations. Balukh et al. 2024 call the same language 'Modo'.

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, penultimate (penultimate stress), not strict' matches the deciding source exactly: Balukh et al. 2024 p. 526 says primary stress 'typically' falls on the penult regardless of word length, enclitics are stressless and outside the domain (stress stays on the root penult), 4-syllable compounds keep penult primary with initial secondary, and a few words surface with final stress at phrase level ([lo.ˈwã], [suˈᵐba]) -- hence dominant rather than strict is right. The quotation is verbatim in the publisher PDF (downloaded now; it was not previously held despite the cite saying 'downloaded and read'). The source is a 2024 peer-reviewed phonological sketch from original fieldwork and is the best available: Glottolog has only two 1987 Indonesian Pusat Bahasa sketches, and no instrumental or other prosodic study exists. Housekeeping only: fill loc = 'p. 526', add DOI 10.25077/ar.1
